To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the formula feeding of term and preterm infants increases biosynthesis of long-chain polyunsaturates, and that the addition of long-chain polyun-saturates to formula reduces the biosynthesis of these fatty acids to breast milk levels.

infant formula potentiates docosaexaenoic/araichidonate (DHA/AA) biosynthesis in term/preterm neonates compared to breastfed neonates and that inclusion of DHA and AA in preterm formulae partially restores DHA and AA biosynthesis to breastfed levels, suggesting that current formulae DHA/AA concentrations are inadequate to achieve normal long-chain PUFA biosynthesis.
formula-fed term and preterm infants have significantly greater biosynthesis/accretion rates for DHA and ARA than breast-fed term and pre-term infants.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the role of dietary fats in the development of the brain and retina in infants.
how the brain develops and how it is affected by nutrition and disease.
understanding the factors that regulate the synthesis and utilization of long-chain polyunsaturates (LC-PUFA) in the developing human.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

formula feeding increases the synthesis/accretion of long-chain polyunsaturates in term and pre-term infants, and that the inclusion in formula of the long-chain polyunsaturation precursors DHA and ARA partially attenuates this effect.
formula-fed infants, term and preterm, synthesize more DHA than breast-fed infants and that the DHA content of current formula is too low to normalize DHA synthesis.

DHA and ARA biosynthesis is significantly enhanced in preterm and term infants fed standard formula compared to breast-fed infants, and that the inclusion in preterm formula of DHA and AHA partially restores DHA and AAR biosynthesis to lower levels.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the formula potentiates biosynthesis of DHA and ARA in term and pre-term neonates compared to breast-fed neonates.
the inclusion of long-chain polyunsaturates in infant formula partially attenuated the excess biosynthesis that occurred in the formula-fed groups.
formula-fed neonates have a greater accretion of long-chain polyunsaturates (LC-PUFA) than breast-fed neonates, and this is true for both preterm and term infants.
The main takeaway from our work is that
formula feeding potentiates DHA/ARA synthesis.
the inclusion of dietary DHA/ARA partially attenuates excess DHA/ARA synthesis in formula-fed preterm and term neonates.
formula feeding increases the synthesis of long-chain polyunsaturates, and that DHA and ARA are synthesized from their precursors, α-linolenic and linoleic acid.
